notes:
CW-044 (Redbrook Coffee Roasters) completed end to end in a single pass and closed two long-standing defects at once. A-133 is fixed - the capital lease amortizes properly now, with Term and Scheduled principal columns added for both instruments. A-132 is fixed - the owner appears once, in the roster and in the narrative. Rent and the lease separated cleanly with no correction needed.

THE NEW FINDING IS A-136 AND IT IS THE KIND THIS PROGRAMME EXISTS TO CATCH. The workbook now ships with every formula intact and NO CACHED VALUES. Excel recalculates on open, so a client double-clicking the file sees a complete plan and nothing looks wrong - which is exactly why it could ship unnoticed. Anything that reads the file without a spreadsheet engine sees blanks: preview panes, server-side renders, PDF exports, a lender importing it, and every automated check. Checks B2, the single cell this run was asked to report, is empty in the delivered artifact and only reads OK after recalculation. The boundary is sharp and datable - the last three builds are 162 to 173KB against 254 to 295KB for everything before them, so about a third of each file is missing and it is the values.

A-137 answers the whole-people question and the answer is half. Named people are whole and sourced to the client's own stated wage. The rest-of-team bucket is expanded into three BLS-titled roles at fractional FTE - 1.29 food batchmakers, 0.86 laborers, 0.57 packers - summing to 4.72 against a stated headcount of 6. The dollars are right and the sourcing labels are honest, so this is about how it reads to a client rather than a wrong number.

Two smaller things worth a glance, both recorded rather than filed: the Q1 debt block shows a NEGATIVE extra principal of -1,163.75, which is arithmetically coherent once you see the 40,536 of new borrowing the model takes under the debt funding preference, but reads oddly on a client-facing schedule; and one ordinary sentence about covering four staff as a group produced 'I had trouble applying that change', which cleared on rephrasing. v33 (CW-045, Thornfield Supply Co., ecommerce): A-138 enters at rank 1 and supersedes A-130 in scope - the rent field is a catch-all sink for any unplaced second dollar figure, hit three times in one intake, and the displaced figure is destroyed rather than misfiled. A-139 and A-140 are new. A-136 could not be retested: the remote-devices bridge was down for the whole run so no file was opened. A-133 (capital lease never amortises) stays FIXED - the lease amortised cleanly at 1,400 a period to zero. A-134's intermediate-state rule was vindicated twice more: a subscription line that first stored unit_price 400 and a phantom nameless Owner payroll row both resolved on a single client correction. v34 (CW-046, Bellamy Row, pre-revenue startup, zero debt): A-141 and A-142 enter at ranks 1 and 2 and are the same failure seen from two ends - the build injects an unrequested 134,180 Sales Manager into a three-person startup whose owner had just declined added roles, and the resulting plan fails its own acceptance gate 16/18 while every client-facing surface reads OK. A-143 and A-144 are new. A-136 and A-139 are CLOSED on file evidence, the first file-level verification since CW-044. A-138 was not reproduced, but by avoidance: the run deliberately used one dollar figure per answer, which starves the rent sink rather than testing it.

recommendations.persona: any client who tells the app their team is complete - and every small business, which is most of them
recommendations.business: Bellamy Row (CW-046)
recommendations.why: THE BUILD ADDS HEADCOUNT THE CLIENT EXPLICITLY DECLINED. Bellamy Row is a three-person pre-revenue handbag label. The client named all three people, and when the app proposed two future hires she replied 'please drop both of those suggested future roles - there are three of us and that is the whole team for the first year.' The app said 'Got it - updated' and cleared them from people_json, which ends holding exactly the three named people. The BUILT Payroll Schedule then carries a fourth role that was never discussed: 'Sales Managers', staffed role, wage source 'Market median for this title (BLS)', annual wage 134,180 - nearly double the owner's own pay - at 0.5 FTE from Q1, ramping to 0.75 at Q5 and 1.00 by Q9. WHY IT IS A BLOCKER: it costs 20,462.45 a quarter, pushing total payroll to 307,550 against the stated 185,000, a 66 percent overshoot rising to 132,599 a quarter by Q20. It converts a plan the intake described as keeping 37,444 a quarter into SIX consecutive negative-EBITDA quarters (-21,667 / -18,772 / -13,342 / -5,488 / -4,429 / -3,221). And it is substantively absurd: a sales-manager role in a direct-to-consumer web shop with no wholesale, no stockists and no sales function, in a business whose owner had just said marketing is the Marketing Lead's job. THEORY, marked as such: this is generated by the capacity labour model rather than from the roster - the sheet prints 'Capacity Units per Supporting FTE = 780' and the role's FTE steps up in lockstep with capacity growth, which would explain both why the title is unconstrained by the actual work and why an explicit client instruction did not bind it.
recommendations.what_to_do: An explicit client statement that the team is complete must bind the build, not just the intake record. Where a capacity model concludes that supporting FTE is needed, it should surface that as a flagged assumption the client can see and refuse, with a title drawn from the work the business actually does - not silently materialise a six-figure BLS role inside the payroll. At minimum, any staffed role with no intake provenance should be visible on a client-facing sheet and named as an app assumption.
recommendations.evidence: Payroll Schedule rows 63-74 and role feed rows 79-126. FINMO Payroll row 14: 46,250 stub (= stated 185,000 / 4, exactly right) then 76,887.45 every forecast quarter. Filed as build_injects_unrequested_high_wage_role_after_client_declined_added_roles.

recommendations.persona: any plan that fails its acceptance gate
recommendations.business: Bellamy Row (CW-046)
recommendations.why: THE PLAN FAILED ITS OWN ACCEPTANCE GATE AND SHIPPED LOOKING FINE. Diagnostics reads: Acceptance Gate Score 16/18, Verdict FAILED, with X on realism_gate_no_hard_fail_violations and viability_timeline_landed, and GPT Exhaustion Handler Fired Yes / Status failed_precondition / Scope pnl_path. Every surface a client actually looks at contradicts it: Checks B2 = OK, Checks A2 'Model Status' = OK, 197 OK / 6 MATCH / 4 CHANGED and ZERO FAIL rows across 230 status cells, books balancing in all periods, and an intake close that told the client in plain English 'your numbers clear every structural test we can run right now' with a mature quarter keeping 37,444 (17.7 percent of revenue). The delivered model instead loses money for six quarters. THIS IS THE EXACT SCENARIO CW-036 WAS COMMISSIONED TO GUARD AGAINST - 'what must NOT happen: a plan that failed acceptance shipping silently as if it passed' - and it has now happened, observed end to end at the artifact.
recommendations.what_to_do: Decide the contract: either a FAILED gate blocks delivery, or the failure surfaces where the client will see it - Cover, Dashboard and Checks - with the reason in plain language. The Checks tab calling itself Model Status and reporting OK on a plan the system judged FAILED is the sharpest edge of this; at minimum Checks should consume the acceptance verdict. Also worth investigating whether the exhaustion handler firing with failed_precondition is itself the fall-through path that lets a failed gate ship.
recommendations.evidence: Diagnostics sheet, Bellamy Row -- 09-07-2026 22-40-44.xlsx. Draft 8e344736a08d493298ce2334746d0c6c, planning run 670df64e79aa46b0a12d5657f103f533. Filed as plan_failed_acceptance_gate_but_shipped_with_every_client_visible_surface_reading_ok.

recommendations.persona: any client who answers a money question with more than one number - which is most of them
recommendations.business: Thornfield Supply Co. (CW-045), and retrospectively Halbrook (CW-041, CW-042)
recommendations.why: THIS IS THE MECHANISM BEHIND A-130, AND IT IS WORSE THAN A-130 DESCRIBED. monthly_rent_expense is not being contaminated by the lease question specifically. It is the extraction target of last resort: when a client's answer yields more dollar figures than the current question has slots, the surplus figure is written to rent. CW-045 hit it three times in one intake on three unrelated questions. (1) Other-monthly-bills question, answer gave 4,500 for utilities/software/insurance and separately about 7,000 for shipping, packaging and card processing - app replied 'It looks like you mean monthly rent - I've set it to 7,000', rent went 3,800 to 7,000. (2) Monthly-debt-payments question, answer gave 'about 3,400 all in - roughly 2,700 on the loan and around 700 on the lease' - app replied 'Recorded: monthly rent 2,700'. (3) A client message that said, in the same sentence, 'the shipping, packaging and card processing at about 7,000 a month - it got mistaken for rent earlier' - and it was written to rent again. An explicit disclaimer in the sentence does not stop it. WHY IT IS A BLOCKER RATHER THAN A NUISANCE: rent survived this run only because the client noticed and corrected it twice. A client who does not audit their own intake ships a plan with the wrong rent. Worse, the displaced figure is not merely misfiled, it is DESTROYED - the 84,000 a year of stated fulfilment cost went nowhere, appears in no line of the built P&L (year-1 lines are Marketing 98,703, Lease/Rent 45,600, Payroll 265,012, G&A 54,517), and overstates net income by roughly half: 156,557 reported against about 72,500 real. The app twice offered 'tell me which line it belongs to and I'll move it', was told twice, and never placed it.
recommendations.what_to_do: Stop treating monthly_rent_expense as an assignable default. A figure should only reach rent from the rent question or from an answer that names rent. Where an answer yields a surplus labelled figure the extractor cannot place, the correct behaviours in order are: route it by the client's own label, ask which line it belongs to and hold it pending, or drop it with a visible note - never silently overwrite an already client-captured field. Also worth an invariant: once a field has wage_source/value_source of client_override from its own question, later turns should not be able to rewrite it without the client naming that field.
recommendations.evidence: CW-045 monthly_rent_expense trace: 3800, 7000, 3800 (client corrected), 2700, 3800 (client corrected), 7000. Three issues filed under signatures rent_overwritten_by_unrelated_opex_figure and monthly_rent_expense_is_default_sink_for_any_second_dollar_figure. Built P&L confirms the missing fulfilment line.

recommendations.persona: any business whose team is given as a group total rather than named people
recommendations.business: any business with more staff than it names individually
recommendations.why: NEW, minor, and the answer to the whole-people question. NAMED people are handled correctly: Head Roaster shows ending FTE 1.00 at the stated 61,000 and Owner 1.00 at 82,000, both labelled 'Your stated wage'. The rest-of-team bucket - one figure of 150,000 covering four staff - is expanded into three BLS-titled roles at FRACTIONAL headcount: Food Batchmakers 1.29 at 36,010, Laborers and Freight/Stock/Material Movers 0.86 at 40,080, and Packers and Packagers Hand 0.57 at 28,970, each labelled 'Market median for this title (BLS)'. Total Ending FTE comes to 4.72 in Q1 against a client-stated headcount of 6. The sourcing labels are honest and the payroll dollars land correctly, so this is a presentation question rather than a wrong number: a client reading the Payroll tab sees 1.29 food batchmakers where they told the app they employ four people. Decide whether the derived block should round to whole heads, or whether the fractional FTE should be presented as an allocation of hours rather than as a count of people.
retests: Any persona that gives a rest-of-team total. Read the Payroll Schedule role blocks and compare summed ending FTE against financials_json.current_num_employees.

recommendations.persona: n/a - a PROCESS finding, not a persona
recommendations.business: the testing programme itself
recommendations.why: NEW - the most valuable non-defect result in several cycles, and it should change how kill-early is applied. CW-043 ran the identical persona and answers that killed CW-042, under a mandate to report rather than stop, and the A-132 owner duplicate reproduced EXACTLY: two roster rows and payroll 190,000 immediately after the owner answer, four rows and 314,000 after the crew leads, and the phantom second-owner paragraph in the key-people narrative. It then HEALED at the very next substantive turn - the narrative correction - collapsing to three properly-titled rows and exactly 219,000, then settling at 599,000 after rest-of-team. CW-042 was killed ONE TURN before the heal. The same pattern applies to CW-041: A-130's rent overwrite still occurs, but the app now announces it and offers to move it, and a single correction restored 5,200 which then held through submit and into the workbook at 15,600 a quarter. TWO RUNS were spent on findings that resolve before anything ships. PROPOSED RULE, for Nick to ratify: kill-early stays for crashes, permanent hangs and anything that makes the run physically impossible; mid-intake stored values are treated as intermediate until the stage closes, and a discrepancy is only a finding if it survives into the SUBMITTED model or the built workbook. Confirmation runs whose objective is an artifact should default to report-do-not-stop. Note the cost asymmetry: killing early saves perhaps twenty minutes; not reaching the artifact cost this programme two full runs and left four targets untested for three cycles.
retests: Applies to every future run. The practical check is simply: does the discrepancy still exist in financials_json at intake_complete, and in the built workbook.

recommendations.persona: the testing programme itself, not the app
recommendations.business: process
recommendations.why: PROCESS RULE, and a companion to A-134. planning_last_heartbeat_at FREEZES during the quarter_grid_ready stage and this is NOT a hang. In CW-046 it stopped at 22:32:47, about 2.5 minutes into a run, and did not advance for roughly eight minutes across repeated 40-second polls while the stage sat unchanged - then the build completed normally at 22:40:44 and produced a correct 16-sheet workbook. A stale heartbeat is precisely the kind of mid-flight reading that killed CW-041 and CW-042. The only sound liveness tests are the stage advancing, planning_run_status flipping to completed, or a new file appearing in the output directory.
recommendations.what_to_do: Write into PLAYBOOK.md: never treat a frozen planning_last_heartbeat_at as evidence of a hang. Poll planning_stage and the output directory instead, and allow at least 15 minutes at quarter_grid_ready before even considering a stall. Separately, worth asking the app team whether the heartbeat should tick through that stage at all - if it is meant to, it is broken; if it is not, the field is misleading by name.
recommendations.evidence: CW-046 monitoring trace; build started 22:30:14, last heartbeat 22:32:47, completed 22:40:44.

recommendations.persona: any business whose stated marketing budget is well below the industry default
recommendations.business: any business - the Marketing Schedule is now on every workbook
recommendations.why: NEW, minor, first live look at the Marketing Schedule sheet. The sheet itself is good: present as the 16th tab, genuinely populated with retention (0.75), purchases per firm (4.8), cost to acquire a firm, returning versus new firms, spend, marketing percentage, and a sourcing block that labels each input ASSUMPTION or derived and names a 220-firm reachable audience. The fidelity problem is that row 15 is labelled 'Marketing pct agreed in your plan' and described as 'the figure your plan was built on', and it reads 0.02 at the stub but 0.04 in every forecast quarter. Row 16 spend is 5,499.90 at the stub - exactly the 22,000 a year the client stated, divided by four - then 14,000 in Q1 rising to 19,670 by Q6, for a forecast Y1 of about 61,792 against the stated 22,000. The driver is cost-to-acquire jumping from 250 at the stub to about 2,545 from Q1. If that escalation is deliberate it should read as a modelled change; presenting it on a row that tells the client it is the number they agreed is the part to fix.
retests: Any persona that corrects the marketing proposal sharply downward. Compare Marketing Schedule rows 15-17 against financials_json.marketing_total_year1 and marketing_percent_of_revenue, at stub and across forecast Y1.

recommendations.persona: any small business whose payroll is a large share of revenue
recommendations.business: Bellamy Row (CW-046)
recommendations.why: Payroll Schedule row 12 prints 'Target Payroll % of Revenue = 0.32'. Row 22 then computes 0.32 for the stub and 0.54, 0.52, 0.48, 0.44 for Q1-Q4 - a 22-point breach of the sheet's own printed target in the first forecast quarter. The Diagnostics realism check named payroll_percent_of_revenue nonetheless reads pass. The only realism metric that fails is fixed_cost_burden_reduced_or_scaled_by_q11, which is the same distortion viewed from the other end. A metric the workbook prints as a target should be checked against that target, and by its own name.
recommendations.what_to_do: Make payroll_percent_of_revenue test the actual against the printed target rather than against a generic band, so the largest single distortion in a plan is caught by the check that carries its name.
recommendations.evidence: Payroll Schedule rows 12, 17, 22; Diagnostics Realism Check Detail. Filed as payroll_percent_of_revenue_realism_metric_passes_while_breaching_the_sheets_own_stated_target.

recommendations.persona: a business that clears the pre-submit gate but falls below the floor at build time
recommendations.business: any capital-heavy business with thin net margin
recommendations.why: PARTIALLY OBSERVED FOR THE FIRST TIME, and no longer purely theoretical. CW-043 produced a second workbook alongside the main one: 'Halbrook Grounds Management RESTRUCTURE ATTEMPT - viable candidate', 151KB, 16 sheets, with a full Cover reading 'Halbrook Grounds Management (RESTRUCTURE...' and a complete Dashboard. So the restructure net does engage and does emit a labelled artifact. What remains unverified is the part this item has always been about: whether a plan that FAILS acceptance is rescued or fails loud, and what the client is shown. Halbrook passed comfortably, so the restructure candidate here appears to be an exploratory alternative rather than a rescue. The persona this needs is still the one described before - intake economics that clear the gate, with the squeeze arriving only from build-time depreciation and debt service. Now that a restructure artifact is known to be produced and named, the next attempt has something concrete to compare against.

recommendations.persona: any client whose lease bills on a different cadence than the question asks for
recommendations.business: any business with leased equipment, vehicles or extra space
recommendations.why: NEW BLOCKER, and the reason CW-041 was killed. The leased-equipment question asks 'what MONTHLY amount should we use for any leased equipment, vehicles, servers, or additional space you do not own'. This client's mower fleet lease bills QUARTERLY, so the natural answer named both figures: 'about 3,600 a quarter, so call it 1,200 a month'. The app confirmed 'I will use 1,200 for monthly lease commitment beyond main rent. Recorded: monthly rent 3,600.' Verified at the stored field: initial_lease is correctly 1,200, and monthly_rent_expense went from 5,200 - answered and explicitly confirmed several questions earlier - to 3,600, which is verbatim the quarterly lease figure. Rent understated by 19,200 a year in what would have been the delivered plan. Three things make this a deal breaker rather than a nit: the value was ALREADY CONFIRMED, the change was SILENT in the sense that it was announced in the same sentence as the lease confirmation where it reads as a restatement, and the triggering answer was the natural response to the app's own question. THEORY, not asserted, not checked against code: the lease handler parses all currency figures in the answer, consumes 1,200 as the lease, and the un-consumed 3,600 falls through to a rent setter - 3,600 is the only other money figure in the sentence and it landed in rent exactly, with no rounding or transformation. Worth checking alongside it: earlier in the same run the install line briefly carried the maintenance line's capacity and utilization before installs had been discussed. That one self-corrected and is a legitimate intermediate state, but a cross-line value bleed in ops and a cross-field value bleed in financials may share a mechanism.
retests: Re-run the CW-041 persona verbatim. Answer the rent question with one figure, then answer the leased-equipment question with a quarterly lease that also names a monthly equivalent, and read financials_json.monthly_rent_expense before and after. Also try a lease answer containing an annual figure, and an answer naming a deposit as well as a payment.

recommendations.persona: any business that repays its debt inside the forecast
recommendations.business: any business whose debt service reaches zero before quarter 20
recommendations.why: NEW, minor, and the only client-visible defect the production test found. Harrow Lane repays its 42,000 of debt inside the forecast, so annual debt service is 0 from Y3 onward, and the Dashboard DSCR tile renders a raw Excel #N/A to the client. FINMO handles the identical case correctly - row 93 prints a dash, and the sheet documents the convention at row 113 - so two surfaces of the same workbook disagree about how an undefined coverage ratio looks. The cause is deliberate and half-right: Calc row 96 is =IFERROR(IF(ISTEXT(FINMO!X93),NA(),FINMO!X93),NA()), and NA() is exactly what a CHART series wants because it breaks the line instead of plotting a false zero. So do not change the Calc value - wrap the tile. This was found by recalculating the built workbook in the Annual view on Y3, Y4 and Y5; reading the formulas alone would not have surfaced it, because the formula is correct for its primary consumer.
retests: Any persona that clears its debt before quarter 20. Set the Dashboard to Annual and step Y1..Y5, and check every coverage tile - DSCR and interest coverage both feed off debt service.

recommendations.persona: n/a - a standing method change, not a persona
recommendations.business: any interactive feature in a generated workbook
recommendations.why: NEW - a METHOD upgrade earned by this run. A-126 made the built-workbook field check standing, but reading cells and formulas cannot prove that an INTERACTIVE feature works. CW-040 proved the dashboard period toggle by writing three toggle states into the built file (Quarterly/Q1, Quarterly/Q7, Annual/Y3) and recalculating each in headless LibreOffice, then comparing the resliced output: selected index 1/7/3, annual flag 0/0/1, points-in-view 20/20/5, Revenue 125,000 / 135,600 / 565,000, Ending Cash 55,010 / 140,300 / 148,600. That is proof rather than inference, it took about two minutes, and it is what caught A-128 - a defect that only appears in a state the default file never shows. Adopt it for any workbook feature with a control: toggles, selectors, scenario switches, anything with data validation. The rule is simple - if a cell drives other cells, drive it and recalculate.
retests: Every future run that builds. Enumerate the workbook's data validations, exercise at least three states including an edge state, recalculate, and diff.

recommendations.persona: any business that states a debt balance and an interest cost
recommendations.business: any business carrying debt into the plan
recommendations.why: NARROWED BY CW-039 - the dollar-impact half is largely answered, the DISCLOSURE half is the live question. VS's research (docs/MILLGATE_A124_A125_RESEARCH.md) established the rate is genuinely SBA-derived from sba_loan_7a_raw, not a 9 pct literal, and identified the real defect underneath: state never reached the resolver, so Millgate got a NATIONAL median. CW-039 confirms that defect is FIXED - debt_interest_rate_policy.source_detail now carries state 'WI', match_basis exact_naics_6, naics 811111, sample_count 106, median 7.975 pct. And the outcome flipped: where Millgate's national median pushed the rate UP from the client's 7.5 pct to 9.0 pct, Bellweather's state-matched median landed at 7.975 pct against the client's own implied 8.00 pct - 0.025 pp BELOW what they stated. So the mechanism is sound and now correctly keyed. What has not changed is that the substitution is invisible: the client is told 'I will use 7,600 for annual interest payment' and is never told the forecast will re-rate from a lending table. The margin tempering IS disclosed at intake close, in plain language, and that is the precedent. Decide whether the rate substitution gets the same sentence.
retests: Any debt-carrying persona. Read derived_driver_policies.debt_interest_rate_policy for state and match_basis, compare annual_rate_decimal against the client's stated interest over stated debt, and scan the delivered plan for any mention of the substitution. The plumbing is fixed; what is being retested is whether the client is told.

recommendations.persona: any
recommendations.business: Thornfield Supply Co. (CW-045)
recommendations.why: The app told the client 'One note: I haven't recorded other operating costs yet - we'll get to that in a moment' while holding other_operating_expense 4500 and other_opex_absolute 54000, both set several turns earlier from the client's own answer and acknowledged at the time with 'Got it - I'll use 4,500 for other operating expense'. Denying possession of a value it is currently holding misdirects the client away from real corrections and invites a duplicate answer that would overwrite or double-count. Minor on its own, but it appeared in the same turn as a rent overwrite, so a client trying to audit their intake is being given two wrong signals at once.
recommendations.what_to_do: Derive these 'not yet recorded' assurances from stored state rather than from the stage plan.
recommendations.evidence: Backend at the moment of the claim: other_operating_expense=4500, other_opex_absolute=54000. Filed as app_denies_holding_a_value_it_already_stored_and_acknowledged.

recommendations.persona: any business whose HR section names individual salaries
recommendations.business: any business with named people and a stated payroll total
recommendations.why: DOWNGRADED IN URGENCY BY CW-039, still worth a ruling. The shape recurs but far smaller and in the opposite direction: Bellweather's stated payroll 226,000 against forecast Y1 227,735, +0.8 pct, versus Millgate's -1.14 pct - and critically the STUB column is exact at 56,500 = 226,000/4. So the headcount schedule tracks the stated total closely and the Millgate gap looks like the tail of the distribution rather than a systematic understatement. The open question is unchanged and is a policy question, not a bug report: when the HR narrative names individual salaries and the P and L is derived from a headcount schedule, is the narrative a contract with the reader? Two runs now say the numbers land within about a percent either way, which argues for wont-fix unless a lender-facing reconciliation is expected.
retests: Any run with two or more named people. Sum the salaries the HR narrative states and compare against finmo_json.pl Payroll for forecast Y1, and compare ending_fte against financials_json.current_num_employees.

recommendations.persona: any
recommendations.business: any business whose plan run fails
recommendations.why: MAJOR, and now VERIFIED after sitting unverified since CW-021. CW-036 is the first failed plan run in thirteen runs and it confirms the behaviour live: planning_run_status is failed with a precise diagnostic, and the client-facing page still reads 'Submitted. Intake submitted successfully. Reference code QJFYJVW77168301424. We are building your plan now - we will review it and follow up with next steps.' A sweep of the rendered page for fail, error, problem and went wrong returns nothing. Stated as two sentences: the BACKEND fails loud and correctly; the CLIENT-FACING SURFACE shows unqualified success. So the strict silent-ship-failed bug did not occur - nothing shipped - but the client is told a plan is being built that is never coming, which is the same harm from their seat. Pairs naturally with A-119: the client who hits that blocker experiences it as an indefinite wait with no signal.

recommendations.persona: any business that reaches a built workbook
recommendations.business: any business, as a standing check rather than a single run
recommendations.why: NEW - a PROGRAMME GAP, not a defect. CW-038 is the first run in thirty-eight to verify a delivered P and L and balance sheet against the numbers the client actually stated, because every prior run either parked, was blocked, or died before the builder. That single pass produced both of this run's findings, and both live in the forecast layer that no earlier run could see. The opening balance sheet was exact to the dollar on all seven client-stated items and the books balanced in 21 of 21 periods, so the layer is broadly sound - but the sample is one. Make the built-workbook check a standing part of the per-run cycle wherever a build completes: opening balance sheet against every stated balance, each expense line against its stated basis for forecast Y1 as well as the baseline period, and an explicit look at which levers carry an applied_by_target_solver_quarters annotation versus which move without one. The solver annotation turned out to be the honest signal that separated the General and Administrative trim, which was disclosed and not filed, from the interest re-rating, which was not.
retests: Every future run that builds. This replaces spot-checking the built plan with a fixed field list.

recommendations.persona: any business that reaches a built workbook
recommendations.business: any business with opening PPE
recommendations.why: NEW, note-severity, surfaced by the first standing use of the A-126 field check. The today/stub column runs a FULL quarter of activity - revenue 175,000, COGS 59,500, marketing 3,000, lease 12,600, payroll 56,500, G and A 10,500, all three months' worth - but books ZERO depreciation, while every forecast quarter books about 9,315 on the same 185,000 of opening PPE. The visible consequence is that stub net income reads 22,648 and the first forecast quarter reads 15,940, and roughly 9,300 of that drop is depreciation appearing rather than anything changing in the business. The same shape was present in CW-038 (stub depreciation 0 against 13,066 in forecast quarters), so this is a deliberate convention rather than an accident, and docs/STUB_CELLS_WHY_RESEARCH.md plus docs/STUB_PURITY_AND_ANNOTATIONS_RESEARCH.md suggest it has already been reasoned about. Filed so the cross-column comparability question gets an explicit ruling: either the stub is a full operating quarter and should carry that quarter's depreciation, or it is an opening snapshot and should not carry a full quarter of revenue and opex either. Right now the two halves of the column are on different bases.
retests: Any run with meaningful opening PPE that builds. Compare finmo pl Depreciation values[0] against values[1] and check whether stub net income is comparable to the first forecast quarter on the same basis.

recommendations.persona: any
recommendations.business: any business that takes a price or rate lever and then builds
recommendations.why: REACHED AT LAST, and the retention number was APPLIED EXACTLY - this closes the intake/remediation half after seven unreachable runs. CW-036 got there legitimately: accepting price rises to the market ceiling triggered the app's own question, 'do you think your current customers would mostly stay with you? recommendations.persona: any
recommendations.business: any business whose stated utilization sits above the expansion ceiling
recommendations.why: NEEDS A PRODUCT DECISION, then possibly a fix. The built plan re-bases a client-stated capacity without telling her. She said 40 landscaping jobs a week at 95 pct; the workbook carries 54.3 a week at 70 pct and runs mature quarters at 538-566 jobs against her stated 520 ceiling, peaking 8.8 pct above what she said she can produce. The mechanism is a policy block with utilization_ceiling 0.85 and post_expansion_utilization 0.7 - any client who states utilization above 0.85 will hit this, which makes it common rather than exotic. The design case is strong: Q1 is a pure re-expression at identical volume, the expansion is funded well ahead of the volume it supports (volume +9.0 pct against payroll +35.5 pct), the row is marked derived_driver payroll_supported_capacity so section 6 makes the workbook truth, and the client explicitly asked for crew growth. The case against is equally simple: those are fields she answered directly, and a search of model_input and operating_model for 'add a crew', 'expand capacity', 'capacity expansion', 'utilization ceiling' and 'running at 95' returns nothing, so she is never told. Cheapest resolution is probably disclosure rather than a model change - one plain sentence at the point of capture or in the plan saying 'you told me 40 a week at 95 pct; sustained operation assumes about 54 a week at 70 pct, which means roughly N more crew' - which would convert this from a silent rewrite into an assumption she can accept or reject. Ranked 1 because it is the only open question from the confirming run and it gates whether the A3 cap is considered working.

closed_this_cycle.why: NEW, major, and a REGRESSION with a datable boundary. The delivered workbook contains every formula but NO CACHED VALUES. Reading Redbrook's file as shipped returns None for Checks B2 and for all 230 Status cells, and blanks across the P and L; reading it for formulas shows a complete, correct model. Recalculating the identical file in headless LibreOffice fills it in and Checks B2 then reads OK with 212 OK, 6 MATCH, 4 CHANGED and zero FAIL - so the model is sound and only the value-caching step is missing. WHY IT MATTERS EVEN THOUGH EXCEL HIDES IT: Excel recalculates on open, so a client double-clicking the file sees numbers and nothing looks wrong. Anything that reads the file without a spreadsheet engine sees an empty workbook - a preview pane, an emailed attachment rendered server-side, a PDF export, a lender importing it, and every automated check this programme runs. It also means Checks B2, the one cell the run was asked to report, is blank in the artifact as delivered. CONFIRMED NOT ISOLATED, and the boundary is sharp: the three most recent builds in the output folder are 162,870 (Redbrook), 172,818 (Willowbank Animal Hospital) and 170,127 (Northgate Systems) bytes, while every earlier build sits between 254,192 and 295,007. Roughly a third of the file is missing and it is the cached values. THEORY, not asserted and not checked against code: the writer path that computes and caches values was skipped or short-circuited recently - the payroll-close work at HEAD d63d5b4 is the change in flight, so it is the first place to look, but the two other undersized builds should date it precisely.
retests: Open any freshly built workbook without a spreadsheet engine and read Checks B2. If it is blank, the cache is missing. The file size alone is a reliable first screen - under about 200KB for a 16-sheet workbook means uncomputed.
